title: Research map
text:
The chain in words

Equilibrium validation (Pillar 1) shows MACE-OFF23 reproduces GFN2-xTB for water — which is what makes the reactive test a real test rather than a foregone conclusion. → motivates
Reactive benchmarking (Pillar 2) finds a ~29 kcal/mol barrier disagreement, then localizes it to the transition-state region and rules out a path-search artifact by evaluating both potentials on identical frozen geometries. The cross-PES saddle search independently validates that the two surfaces have distinct but nearby stationary points. → motivates
Targeted correction (Pillar 3) puts the correction data where the error is, beating an equal-budget generic control, and reaches a certified saddle barrier of 6.33 kcal/mol against an xTB target of 6.7. → motivates
Iterating that correction (Pillar 4) does not keep improving it — iteration 0 remains the best model after 42 further reference calculations — and handing corrected saddles to the reference reaches its TS in only 3 of 6 cases (Study 09). That → motivates a controlled capacity ablation as the next experiment.
Current work (Sn-β hydride transfer) carries the pipeline to a catalytic system with newer foundation models. It is shown in amber because it has no results yet.

title: Pillar 3 — Post-training correction
text: Scientific question Can a lightweight post-training correction adapt a pretrained MACE toward a chosen reference, without fine-tuning the foundation model?

title: Pillar 3 — Post-training correction
text:
Why we tested it
Pillar 2 established two things that together make a correction plausible. First, the disagreement is systematic, not random: force directions already agree (cosine ≈ 0.98) and it is magnitude that is off. Second, it is localized in the transition-state region rather than spread across the surface. A systematic, localized residual is exactly the kind of thing a small model can absorb.
Fine-tuning MACE-OFF23 is deliberately off the table here — the point is to see how far a cheap wrapper gets. Every correction below is applied through a CorrectedCalculator that leaves the foundation model untouched.

Key result Measured as a certified saddle rather than a scan maximum, the targeted Delta gives 6.33 kcal/mol relative to the frozen xTB reactant geometry and 8.23 kcal/mol relative to the reactant relaxed on the corrected model, against an xTB reference of 6.7 — differences of −0.37 and +1.53 kcal/mol. Its reaction mode is at −358.3 cm⁻¹ (xTB: −394) and it sits 0.173 Å (RMSD) from the xTB TS. This is the strongest one-shot correction result in the project.


Why both reactant references matter The frozen reference evaluates the corrected model at the xTB reactant geometry; it asks how the corrected surface scores the reference’s own endpoints. The relaxed reference lets the reactant find its minimum on the corrected surface first, so both ends of the barrier are stationary points of the same model — the stricter internal-consistency check. The 1.9 kcal/mol gap between them is itself a measure of how far the corrected reactant basin still sits from the reference geometry. Neither number replaces the other.


Both numbers are real — they measure different things 9.9 kcal/mol is the constrained-scan estimator and remains the correct value for that quantity; it is what earlier write-ups reported and it has not been withdrawn. 6.33 kcal/mol is the certified saddle on the same model. The scan overestimates by ≈3.5 kcal/mol here because its constrained path misses the saddle by ~0.19 Å in the forming C–C coordinate. Both estimators are tracked separately throughout Study 08; neither replaces the other.

title: Pillar 3 — Post-training correction
section: What counts as a transition state?
text:
What counts as a transition state?
Matching a barrier number is not enough: a scan maximum or an NEB image can sit at the right energy without being a saddle point, and two different surfaces can give the same barrier from different structures. On this site a structure is called a certified first-order saddle only when every step below passes:

Sella saddle search (order = 1) converged, final force below 1e−4 eV/Å.
Finite-difference Hessian of the converged structure (central differences, 1e−3 Å).
Mass-weighted vibrational analysis — frequencies from M^−½ H M^−½, not raw Hessian eigenvalues.
Exactly one significant imaginary mode (below −50 cm⁻¹).
The imaginary mode is the reaction: forming C–C in 1.5–3.0 Å and overlap ≥ 0.30 with the forming-bond coordinate.

Two of the six iterations in Pillar 4 converged in Sella but failed step 4 (two imaginary modes); they are reported as uncertified. The full standard is on the Methods page.

title: Pillar 3 — Post-training correction
text:
What we learned
A lightweight conservative correction, fit only on force residuals and applied without touching the foundation model, can bring the corrected surrogate’s certified saddle to within 0.4 kcal/mol (frozen xTB reactant) or 1.5 kcal/mol (model-relaxed reactant) of the chosen reference — and can do so with data concentrated in the region that actually disagrees, without disturbing the water structure relative to the baseline correction.
Two honest caveats. The reference here is xTB, which is not ground truth, and no higher-level barrier has been established for this reaction in the project — so this demonstrates reference-matching, not improved physical accuracy. And the corrected saddle still sits 0.173 Å from the xTB one — energetic agreement is better than geometric agreement.
The obvious next question is whether the same targeting trick keeps paying off when iterated. That is Pillar 4.

title: Pillar 1 — MACE ↔︎ xTB validation
text:
Why we tested it
The whole programme depends on replacing an expensive reference with a cheap surrogate. xTB scales roughly O(N³) while a message-passing potential scales ~linearly, so the surrogate only becomes worthwhile if it is both faster at size and faithful at equilibrium. This pillar establishes the baseline: if agreement failed here, nothing downstream would be interpretable.
MACE-OFF23 is trained on DFT (ωB97M-D3BJ), not on xTB. Agreement is therefore two independent methods converging, not a fit.

title: Pillar 1 — MACE ↔︎ xTB validation
text:
What we learned
Equilibrium agreement is strong enough to build on, and the cost crossover means the surrogate is worth using at the sizes we care about. This is the licence to ask the harder question: agreement on a smooth equilibrium basin says nothing about a bond-breaking event, where the potential must extrapolate far from its training distribution. That is Pillar 2.

Method control An early MD benchmark appeared to show ~2817 ms/step. That was CPU contention from concurrent downloads, not a real cost; a clean re-benchmark gives ~37 ms/step. The original misleading number is retained in Study 05 rather than deleted.

title: ML-Accelerated Metadynamics
text:
The project in six answers


What are we trying to do? Run enhanced sampling (metadynamics) on a machine-learned surrogate while keeping the accuracy of the quantum-chemical reference it replaces — and know, with evidence, where that substitution holds and where it does not.


Why pretrained MACE with enhanced sampling? Metadynamics needs long trajectories of force evaluations. A pretrained MACE model (MACE-OFF23 here) is cheap per step and scales roughly linearly, while the reference (GFN2-xTB) does not: MACE’s measured cost relative to xTB falls from 2.5× to 1.0× between 60 and 150 atoms. On equilibrium water it already reproduces the reference. Pillar 1


What did the Diels–Alder benchmark reveal? Force directions agree closely along the reaction path (mean cosine 0.982) and the two potentials place the transition state in the same region — but they describe a materially different reactive surface: MACE’s barrier is 35.8–37.2 kcal/mol depending on the estimator, against 6.7 for xTB. The difference is concentrated at the transition state and survives every methodological control. Pillar 2


What did targeted correction accomplish? A conservative pairwise correction, trained mostly on barrier-region data and applied without touching the foundation model, brings the certified saddle to 6.33 kcal/mol against the frozen xTB reactant geometry, or 8.23 kcal/mol against the reactant relaxed on the corrected model — versus 6.7 for xTB. Pillar 3


What failed or remains unresolved? Repeating the correction with more targeted reference data did not keep improving it: the scan barrier degraded from 9.87 to 13.91 kcal/mol over 42 extra reference calculations. Handing corrected-model saddles to the reference optimizer reached the reference transition state in only 3 of 6 cases, and no tested descriptor predicted which. Pillar 4


What are we testing next? Whether the newer MACE-OMOL and MACE-POLAR foundation models give a useful starting surface for a catalytic reaction — the Sn-β-catalysed glucose C2→C1 hydride transfer. The pipeline is built and tested; the authoritative structures are not yet in hand, so there are no results yet. Current work

Findings
Each pillar is a 2–4 minute read. The detailed Studies remain the source of truth for methodology, full tables, and controls; the Methods page defines every estimator used below.


PILLAR 1

Equilibrium validation
Does off-the-shelf MACE-OFF23 reproduce GFN2-xTB for equilibrium water?
Demonstrated Yes. Forces correlate at r = 0.991–0.992 and MD reproduces the O–O structure.



PILLAR 2

Reactive benchmark
Does that agreement survive bond-forming chemistry?
Demonstrated Only partly. Force directions and TS region agree; barriers differ by 29–31 kcal/mol, a genuine difference between the two surfaces.



PILLAR 3

Targeted correction
Can a lightweight correction close the gap without retraining?
Demonstrated Largely, once. Certified saddle 6.33 (frozen xTB reactant) / 8.23 (model-relaxed reactant) vs xTB 6.7 kcal/mol.



PILLAR 4

Iteration and handoff
Does more targeted data, or handing off to the reference, keep improving it?
Negative result No. Iteration 0 stayed the best model; only 3 of 6 handoffs reached the reference TS.

title: ML-Accelerated Metadynamics
text:
The scientific chain
Each step exists because the previous one raised a specific question:

Equilibrium agreement is strong — which makes the reactive test meaningful rather than a foregone conclusion.
Reactive agreement fails, and the failure is localized to the transition-state region — which motivates correcting there rather than globally.
Targeted correction works, once — which raises the follow-up: does it keep working if iterated, and can the corrected model hand off to the reference?
It does not, and no handoff signal was found — which points at correction capacity, rather than reference-data quantity, as the next thing to test.

The Research Map shows how the individual studies attach to this chain.

title: ML-Accelerated Metadynamics
text:
What we learned

Demonstrated A pretrained MACE model can agree closely with a reference at equilibrium and still represent a materially different reactive surface. Equilibrium validation does not license reactive use.
Demonstrated Matching a barrier is not the same as matching a saddle: scan maxima, NEB images, and certified saddles on the same model differ by up to 3.5 kcal/mol, and the reactant reference moves the result by another 1.9 kcal/mol.
Demonstrated Where the correction data goes matters more than how much there is — at equal budget, barrier-region data moved the barrier; generic data did not.
Interpretation The failure of iteration is consistent with a capacity limit of a radial pairwise correction. This is a hypothesis, not a result.
Open question Whether a richer correction converges on the same budget — and whether the newer MACE-OMOL / MACE-POLAR models start closer for catalytic chemistry.


Reference, not ground truth GFN2-xTB is the chosen alignment target, not ground truth. This project has not established a higher-level (DFT or experimental) barrier for this reaction, so which surface is physically closer is not assessed here. Matching xTB is reference-matching, never “improved accuracy”.

title: Study 09 — Reference handoff: cost and diagnostics
text:
Scientific question Given the Phase C corrected model and the iterative loop of Pillar 4, does handing a corrected-model saddle to Sella on the GFN2-xTB surface reduce the reference cost of reaching the verified xTB transition state — and is there an observable that says when to hand off?
Two linked experiments (Aug 21), both negative. Full write-ups: handoff benchmark · handoff diagnostics. All numbers below are read from sweep/corrections/aug21_handoff/results.json and sweep/corrections/aug21_diagnostics/*.json.

title: Study 09 — Reference handoff: cost and diagnostics
text:
Method

Same settings for every case: Sella, Cartesian coordinates, order = 1, fmax = 1e−4 eV/Å, 500 steps, on GFN2-xTB (electronic temperature 1000 K, 500 SCF iterations), run with sella 2.5.0 — the version used in Phase 2.
Cost metric: genuine Calculator.calculate() calls counted inside the xTB calculator (one call = one SCF giving energy and forces). Sella’s nsteps undercounts by 1.0–2.0× in these runs and is kept only as a cross-check.
Accounting: candidate n has a prior adaptive cost of 7n reference calls from the loop. The 106 Phase C training references are a separate sunk cost. Hessian certification (96 calls per case) is excluded from every case alike.
Baseline: the xTB-only route — a sequential relaxed scan from the reactant, then Sella from the scan maximum.
Control: an IDPP-interpolated guess, which costs no reference calls to produce.

Key result — negative Only 3 of 6 handoffs reached the TS, with no trend in iteration number (successful totals 97, 50, 104 at n = 0, 1, 5; failures at n = 2, 3, 4). The baseline’s cost is dominated by its scan (547 of 582 calls), and a zero-cost IDPP guess reaches the same TS in 75 calls. Measured against that cheapest working alternative, only one handoff (iteration 1, 50 calls) is cheaper, and nothing identified it in advance.


What “failed” means here Iterations 2 and 4 reach the right structure — forming C–C 2.3153 Å, 0.0016 Å RMSD from the xTB TS, 6.71 kcal/mol — but never tighten below the pre-registered fmax = 1e−4 within 500 steps (they reach 1e−3 in 45 and 54 steps, like the successes). Iteration 3 is the only genuine wrong-basin failure: it converges to a reactant-basin stationary point (forming C–C 3.74 Å, −0.20 kcal/mol, reaction-mode overlap 5e−5). The threshold was not loosened after the fact; this is reported as threshold sensitivity, not a redefinition of the result.

Every successful run lands on the same structure: forming C–C 2.3153 Å, 6.71 kcal/mol, principal imaginary mode −393.4 cm⁻¹ — the verified xTB TS (2.315 Å, 6.7 kcal/mol, −394 cm⁻¹).

text:
Caveats

One reaction, one system, one correction family.
The 547-call scan cost depends on the sequential relaxed-scan protocol chosen.
Strict Hessian certification is unreliable on the xTB surface here. Identical structures (same forming distance, barrier, and −393.4 cm⁻¹ principal mode) intermittently show 1–3 imaginary modes because soft reactant-side van der Waals modes sit near the 50 cm⁻¹ cutoff. The benchmark therefore reports reached the reference saddle (structure and principal-mode identity) separately from strict Hessian cleanliness.
This is not active learning: the loop used a fixed, hand-specified query rule with no acquisition function or uncertainty estimate.
A prediction made before the experiment — that the IDPP control would fail — was wrong.

…and reveals a bias-scaling artifact
Raising kpush from 0.008 → 0.05 at n = 30 barely perturbs the droplet. That is not intrinsic robustness: the bias is a function of global RMSD spread over all degrees of freedom, so the same nominal kpush is far gentler on a 90-atom droplet than on a dimer.

title: Study 01 — Bias × size
text:
Sweeping bias strength kpush against cluster size shows the RMSD bias preferentially rips whatever bond is weakest. A lone water resists and only dissociates at high bias — it has to break a covalent O–H (~5 eV). Hydrogen-bonded clusters come apart even at the lowest bias, because the intermolecular H-bond (~0.2 eV) snaps first. The tetramer is the most robust, held by more H-bonds.



Fraction of the 20 ps run each cluster stayed intact (one fragment, all O–H present). Reading across a row, more bias breaks clusters sooner.








TipTakeaway



What breaks depends on what holds the system together: a global-RMSD bias just maximizes structural novelty, and the cheapest way to do that is to snap the weakest bond — which for clusters means evaporation, not rearrangement.

That the errors concentrate in the distorted barrier region is directly measured here. text:
4 · Methodological controls
The obvious objection to the ~30 kcal/mol gap: MACE used NEB, xTB used its built-in path search, so maybe the gap is a path-method mismatch. Three controls close that off.

MACE’s barrier is method-invariant
Across the constrained relaxed scan (36.05), the CI-NEB highest image (37.20), and the Sella saddle refined from it (36.2), MACE gives the same answer to within 1.2 kcal/mol. The CI-NEB highest image is also stable with respect to image count — 35.9 ± 1.0 kcal/mol for ≥11 NEB images (9 images is too few: the barrier collapses to ~18 and the TS drifts to 2.5 Å) — although none of these runs recorded whether the band optimization itself converged, and the 13-image band contains one collapsed image that the analysis excluded. The converged estimators are the relaxed scan and the Sella saddles.



Highest-image barrier vs NEB image count: stable for ≥11 images; 9 is under-resolved. Band-optimization convergence was not recorded for these runs.




The xtb-python stability gate
Before running xTB through the same NEB driver, the backend was gated: single-points, forces, and geometry optimization are reproducible, with repeat-evaluation energy scatter of 5.08e−14 eV (machine precision), a converged optimization at fmax 0.021, and ~4.4 ms per call. The robust settings (electronic_temperature=1000, max_iterations=500, accuracy=1.0) do not perturb path energetics.

title: Study 04 — Diels–Alder reaction
text:
6 · Final interpretation
Directly demonstrated. On identical frozen geometries the two potentials disagree by 21.2 kcal/mol on the barrier; the xTB TS is not a MACE stationary point (1.84 eV/Å); Sella from that TS converges to a genuine first-order MACE saddle 0.316 Å away at 35.8 kcal/mol, matching the independent NEB result; and that saddle is robustly recovered from ±0.05 Å perturbations with zero barrier spread.
Supported interpretation. The two surfaces describe nearby but distinct saddle regions. The barrier disagreement is intrinsic to the potentials rather than an artifact of methodology or convergence.
Not demonstrated. Which method is physically more accurate cannot be settled from this experiment: no higher-level (DFT or experimental) reference has been established for this reaction in the project. Nothing here establishes that the foundation model’s training set lacks these geometries, and nothing transfers automatically to other reactions.
Two claims that are easy to conflate stay separate: nearby TS geometry and matching TS energy are different achievements, and this system has the first without the second.

title: Study 06 — kpush should scale with size
text:
xTB’s bias is a Gaussian in root-mean-square deviation, \(V = k_\text{push}\,e^{-\alpha\,\mathrm{RMSD}^2}\) with \(\mathrm{RMSD}^2 = \frac1N\sum_i|x_i-x_i^\text{ref}|^2\). The bias force on an atom,
\[F_i = k_\text{push}\,\alpha\,e^{-\alpha\,\mathrm{RMSD}^2}\,\frac{2}{N}\,(x_i-x_i^\text{ref}),\]
carries an explicit 1/N — the same kpush pushes each atom \(1/N\) as hard in a bigger system. To keep the per-atom bias effect constant, kpush must scale ∝ N (per-atom; per-molecule is the same with \(N=3\times\#\text{waters}\)).



Fixed kpush follows the 1/N line (diluted); N-scaled kpush holds the per-atom force constant across n=3→96 atoms.

title: Study 06 — kpush should scale with size
text:
Empirical confirmation
The trimer first fragments at kpush = 0.008, so the N-scaling predicts the 30-water droplet reaches the same per-atom bias at kpush ≈ 0.008 × 90/9 = 0.08. The droplet is intact up to 0.05 — and at ~0.08 it starts shedding a molecule, right on the prediction.



Intact through kpush 0.05; onset of fragmentation at the N-scaled ~0.08.








NoteCaveat



The onset is soft because size changes two things at once: it dilutes the per-atom force (1/N — corrected here) and raises cohesion (more H-bonds per interior molecule). The kpush ∝ N law fixes the first exactly; the second means a big droplet still resists a bit more than bare force-scaling predicts.


Practical rule: set kpush per atom, kpush_eff = kpush_ref · N / N_ref, so bias strength is comparable across cluster sizes.

title: Study 08 — Post-training corrections
text: This is the detailed study behind Pillar 3 — Post-training correction and Pillar 4 — Iterative calibration. Those pages carry the argument; this page keeps the full tables, controls, and limitations.

title: Study 08 — Post-training corrections
text:
1 · Motivation
The Diels–Alder benchmark (Study 04) showed MACE and xTB agree on force direction but differ in magnitude, localized in the reactive region. A systematic, localized residual is the kind of thing a small model can absorb. The question is whether a lightweight post-training correction — fit on paired MACE/xTB forces, with no foundation-model retraining — can remove it.
Base = MACE-OFF23, target = GFN2-xTB (a cheap stand-in for the eventual DFT reference); all applied through the existing CorrectedCalculator, which leaves the foundation model untouched.

title: Study 08 — Post-training corrections
text:
2 · Correction architectures
Four models: global (F′ = αF), affine (+ energy shift), element (per-element force scaling, non-conservative), and a conservative delta (energy = fitted radial pair potentials, forces = −∇, linear least-squares fit).

Because it is an energy expression differentiated analytically, it is conservative and therefore MD- and metadynamics-safe.

title: Study 08 — Post-training corrections
text:
8 · Limitations and next question
Reference, not truth. xTB is the chosen proof-of-concept target, not ground truth. No higher-level (DFT or experimental) barrier has been established for this reaction in the project, so matching xTB demonstrates reference-matching, not improved physical accuracy.
Energetic before geometric. Even the best corrected saddle sits 0.173 Å from the xTB TS. Energy agreement outran geometry agreement.
Scope. One reaction, one correction family, one acquisition rule, one budget. Nothing here transfers automatically to other systems.
Not demonstrated. No active learning was implemented — no acquisition metric, no uncertainty estimate, no autonomous sampling — so this says nothing about active learning in general. And the pairwise Delta has not been shown incapable of matching the xTB saddle; only that it did not, under this rule and budget.
Next question — is correction-model capacity the bottleneck? Two observations point that way: the Delta is a sum of radial pair potentials with no angular or many-body terms, while a cycloaddition saddle’s position and curvature depend on angular reorganization of the forming ring; and xTB is never near-stationary at the corrected saddle, so force-matching there asks the correction to reproduce a large reference gradient at a point the model believes is stationary. The discriminating experiment holds the acquisition rule fixed and varies expressiveness — angular/three-body terms, a larger cutoff, more radial channels. That behaviour is consistent with a correction-capacity limitation, which is a supported hypothesis, not a demonstrated result.

title: Current work — Sn-β glucose hydride transfer

The question

Scientific question Can MACE-OMOL or MACE-POLAR provide a useful starting potential-energy surface for the Sn-β-catalysed glucose C2→C1 hydride-transfer step — the rate-limiting step of glucose-to-fructose isomerization?

Reference. S. H. Mushrif, J. J. Varghese, C. B. Krishnamurthy, Solvation dynamics and energetics of intramolecular hydride transfer reactions in biomass conversion, Phys. Chem. Chem. Phys. 17, 4961–4969 (2015), DOI 10.1039/C4CP05063K.
The immediate experiment is narrower than the original study: whether these models give a physically meaningful transition pathway between known initial and final states, initially without reproducing the full explicit-solvent metadynamics.

Why new foundation models
MACE-OFF23, used for the Diels–Alder benchmark, was trained on organic chemistry and has no tin. section: What the literature does and does not establish
text:
What the literature does and does not establish
The paper itself is closed access and has not been read in full; the points below come from its abstract and from a thesis that reproduces its Fig. 1 (M. A. Y. Ali, MSc thesis, University of Alberta, 2025). Nothing here has been checked against the paper’s full text.

Literature Protocols. The paper uses CPMD-metadynamics with explicit water or methanol, a CPMD-metadynamics run without solvent, and implicit-solvent DFT (abstract). The thesis’s own dataset is a 20,000-timestep gas-phase run; whether it is the paper’s solvent-free run is not established.
Literature, as drawn Model. The thesis figure adapted from the paper draws the site as a SiH₃-capped Sn cluster, Sn(–O–SiH₃)₃, with open-chain glucose bound through its C1 and C2 oxygens and the water formed at the site remaining on Sn.
Literature, secondary Collective variables. CV1 is the coordination number of C1 with the two hydrogens H1 and H2; CV2 is the coordination number of C2 with the same two hydrogens, using CPMD’s rational coordination function.
Unknown CV parameters d₀, p, q. The project’s code computes these CVs with placeholder parameters that are explicitly flagged as unconfirmed, and refuses to compare against the reference basin values until the originals are supplied.
Unknown Charge and multiplicity — not stated in either source.


Not a reference value The “≈82 kJ/mol barrier” sometimes quoted for this reaction comes from data tips on the thesis’s gas-phase metadynamics free-energy plot, not from a verified published value. It is a free-energy difference from a biased-sampling run; an endpoint-to-endpoint NEB or Sella calculation gives a potential-energy barrier, and the two are not directly comparable.

title: Methods & reproducibility
text: This page exists so that numbers on this site are never compared across estimators or reference states by accident. Every barrier quoted elsewhere names one of the estimators below and the reactant it is measured from.

title: Methods & reproducibility
text:
Estimator glossary


Relaxed-scan maximum (constrained scan)

The highest point along a scan in which the two forming C–C distances are held equal at a sequence of values while every other coordinate relaxes; the barrier is measured from the first scan point. Cheap and robust, but the constrained path need not pass through the true saddle. Used for: raw and corrected Diels–Alder profiles (e.g. 36.05, 11.66, 9.87 kcal/mol).

CI-NEB highest image

The highest-energy physical image of a climbing-image nudged elastic band. An approximation to the saddle: it can carry a second imaginary mode, depends on the image count, and is only as good as the band’s convergence — which must be stated. Used for: raw MACE-OFF23, 37.20 kcal/mol (13 images; band convergence not recorded; one collapsed image excluded); 35.9 ± 1.0 over 11–21 images. A later standardized control recorded non-convergence, so NEB values here are diagnostics only.

Sella-refined saddle

A first-order saddle search (Sella, order = 1) started from a guess — an NEB image, a scan maximum, or another surface’s TS. Converged means the force criterion was met; it is not yet certified. Used for: raw MACE 36.2 (from the NEB image) and 35.81 (from the xTB TS).

Certified first-order saddle

A Sella-refined saddle that also passes every step of the transition-state standard below. Only these are called transition states on this site. Used for: corrected-model saddle 6.33 / 8.23 kcal/mol; iterations 0, 1, 2, 4.

Frozen-reactant reference

The barrier is measured from the model’s energy at the xTB-optimized reactant geometry, without relaxing it on the model being tested. Used for: 6.33 kcal/mol (corrected saddle); 35.81 kcal/mol (raw MACE saddle from the xTB TS).

Model-relaxed reactant reference

The reactant is first relaxed on the model being tested, so both ends of the barrier are stationary points of that model — the stricter internal-consistency check. Used for: 8.23 kcal/mol (same corrected saddle). A related variant relaxes the reactant with the forming bonds pinned, so the weakly bound complex cannot drift apart; used for the raw-MACE CI-NEB and its refined saddle.

Potential-energy barrier

A difference of potential energies between two structures on one surface (no entropy, no temperature). Every Diels–Alder barrier on this site is one.

Metadynamics free-energy surface

The negative of the accumulated bias from a metadynamics run, as a function of the biased collective variables. Its differences are free-energy differences at the simulation temperature, and its absolute levels are arbitrary offsets. Not comparable one-to-one with a potential-energy barrier. (The xTB RMSD-metadynamics runs in Studies 01–03 produce sampled potential-energy landscapes from a biased run, which are neither.)

title: Methods & reproducibility
section: What counts as a transition state
text:
What counts as a transition state
A structure is a certified first-order saddle only if all of the following hold:

Sella saddle search with order = 1 converged to a maximum atomic force below 1e−4 eV/Å (Cartesian coordinates).
Finite-difference Hessian at the converged structure: central differences with a 1e−3 Å displacement, symmetrized.
Mass-weighted vibrational analysis: frequencies are the eigenvalues of M^−½ H M^−½ converted to wavenumbers (ν = 521.47·√λ cm⁻¹ for λ in eV Å⁻² amu⁻¹). Raw Hessian eigenvalues are never converted to frequencies.
Exactly one significant imaginary mode: one frequency below −50 cm⁻¹.
The imaginary mode is the reaction: forming C–C within 1.5–3.0 Å and an overlap of at least 0.30 between the mode’s Cartesian displacement and the forming-bond coordinate.

Matching a barrier number satisfies none of these. A scan maximum, NEB image, or uncertified stationary point is always labelled as such.

Known limitations of the standard On the xTB surface, identical structures intermittently show 1–3 imaginary modes because soft van der Waals modes of the reactant complex sit near the −50 cm⁻¹ cutoff; the handoff benchmark therefore reports reaching the reference saddle separately from strict Hessian cleanliness (Study 09). An early MACE saddle check (Study 04, Phase 1) counted imaginary modes without mass weighting; the count is valid, but its frequency value is not quoted anywhere.

title: Methods & reproducibility
text:
Calculations
Reference — GFN2-xTB. xtb 6.7.1 for metadynamics, built-in path search and Hessians (frequencies read from the vibspectrum file, never parsed from standard output); xtb-python as an ASE calculator for scans, Sella, and force evaluations. Periodic runs use GFN1-xTB, which is a different level of theory.
Surrogates — MACE foundation models as ASE calculators:

MACE-OFF23 (small) for every Diels–Alder and water result; float64 for saddle searches and Hessians, float32 for MD.
MACE-OMOL-0 and MACE-POLAR-1 for the Sn-β work in progress, through a wrapper that always sets total charge and spin multiplicity explicitly.

Correction layer. Every correction is applied through a CorrectedCalculator that wraps the unmodified foundation model. The conservative pairwise Delta is a sum of Gaussian radial basis functions per element pair (8 functions × 6 pair channels = 48 coefficients, 3.6 Å cutoff), fit by ridge least squares (λ = 1e−3) on force residuals F_xTB − F_MACE; its forces are the analytic gradient of its energy, so it is conservative.
Data splits. Correction training and evaluation sets are split by parent path geometry (no leakage between rattled copies of one structure); the iterative loop keeps a fixed 48-configuration held-out reactive set that is never trained on.

title: Methods & reproducibility
text:
Evidence standards
Statements on this site carry one of five labels:

Demonstrated directly measured in a result file of this repository.
Interpretation a supported explanation of a measured result — not itself demonstrated.
Open question not tested.
Work in progress infrastructure built; no scientific result yet.
Literature stated in, or read from a figure of, an external source — not measured here.

And four rules:

Every number traces to a result file or a FINDINGS_*.md in the repository.
xTB is the chosen reference, not ground truth; matching it is reference-matching.
A superseded estimate is shown next to its replacement, never silently replaced.
Negative results are reported plainly.

Equilibrium water samples a smooth basin well inside any potential’s comfort zone. A cycloaddition does the opposite: it drives the system through half-formed bonds and strongly distorted geometries. If a surrogate is going to carry reactive enhanced sampling, this is the regime that decides it.

The obvious objection: MACE used NEB, xTB used its own path search, so perhaps the gap is just a path-method mismatch. Two independent tests close that off.

Robustness. Displacing the MACE saddle by ±0.02 and ±0.05 Å along its imaginary mode and re-running Sella from each of the four perturbed structures recovers the same saddle every time: barrier 35.806 kcal/mol in all four runs (spread 0.000) and RMSD to the reference below 1e−5 Å. The saddle is well isolated, not an optimizer artifact.

Key result MACE-OFF23 keeps strong force-direction agreement and a similar reaction geometry, but represents a materially different reactive surface near the transition state. The barrier disagreement is a genuine difference between the MACE and xTB potential-energy surfaces, not a path-search artifact. The two methods agree on mechanism and place their saddles only 0.316 Å apart, but those are distinct stationary points with very different energies — the xTB TS carries 1.84 eV/Å of MACE force, and MACE’s own saddle sits at 35.8 kcal/mol against xTB’s 6.7.

title: Pillar 2 — Reactive chemistry
text:
What we learned
Same geometry region, same mechanism, different surface. Two claims that are easy to conflate must be kept apart: nearby TS geometry and matching TS energy are separate achievements, and this system has the first without the second.
Because the error is localized rather than global, a correction does not need to repair the whole surface — only the barrier region. That is the premise of Pillar 3.

title: Pillar 4 — Iterative correction and reference handoff
text:
Why we tested it
Pillar 3 showed that a single round of barrier-region data brings the certified corrected saddle to 6.33 kcal/mol against an xTB target of 6.7. The natural next move is a loop: find the current corrected saddle, ask the reference what it thinks there, add that data, refit, and repeat. If that converged, it would be the skeleton of a data-efficient calibration workflow.
The loop was run as a controlled experiment, not an autonomous system: the query rule was fixed by hand, and no acquisition function or uncertainty estimate was involved.

title: Pillar 4 — Iterative correction and reference handoff
text:
One iteration

Relaxed concerted scan on the current corrected surface → scan barrier, and a seed geometry for the saddle search.
Sella first-order saddle search from that seed.
TS validity gate — the structure counts as a Diels–Alder saddle only if it converged, has exactly one imaginary mode, has forming C–C in 1.5–3.0 Å, and its imaginary mode overlaps the forming-bond coordinate by ≥ 0.30.
Query GFN2-xTB at that geometry.
Build a small local packet — the saddle itself, ±0.05 and ±0.10 Å along the imaginary mode, and 2 isotropic 0.05 Å perturbations: 7 new xTB calculations.
Refit the same Delta architecture on the cumulative dataset.

Held fixed throughout: the correction architecture and every hyperparameter, and a 48-configuration held-out reactive split that is never trained on.

Supporting observations:

2 of 6 iterations produced no certifiable first-order saddle (two imaginary modes), and fell back to the scan maximum as the query centre. Their Sella stationary points (8.62 and 9.25 kcal/mol) are not counted as certified barriers. (Earlier write-ups quoted the error trend as 0.37 → 2.55 kcal/mol; the 2.55 endpoint is iteration 5, which is uncertified. The last certified error is 2.76.)
Held-out reactive error worsens slightly: TS+post-TS RMSE 0.6879 → 0.7113 (+3.4%). The added data is not generalizing.

The fit is not diverging. The Delta coefficient norm stays essentially constant (6.05, 5.95, 5.99, 5.97, 5.95, 6.11), so this is a fixed capacity being reallocated, not a numerically unstable regression.


Method control — seeding the saddle search An earlier version of this loop seeded each saddle search from the xTB TS, the strategy that works for raw MACE. On a corrected surface it fails: Sella converges to a spurious reactant-basin saddle at 3.20 Å whose imaginary mode is orthogonal to bond formation (overlap 1.2e−06) and whose “barrier” is −3.84 kcal/mol, below the reactant. That run is retained as a negative control. The fix — seeding from each iteration’s own relaxed-scan maximum, plus the validity gate above — follows the project’s existing convention for saddle searches.


A metric not to over-read The cosine between corrected and xTB forces at a converged saddle is meaningless: the corrected force is ~1e−4 eV/Å there by construction, so the cosine is a 0/0 noise ratio. The interpretable quantity is xTB’s own residual force at the corrected saddle, which oscillates over 0.43–2.81 eV/Å with no systematic decrease.

title: Pillar 4 — Iterative correction and reference handoff
text:
What we learned
More targeted reference data is not automatically better for a fixed correction architecture — and the corrected model’s saddles are not a reliably better handoff point than a cheap geometric guess. For this system the expensive step is generating a starting guess, and an IDPP interpolation already does that well. The result is specific and bounded: this correction form, this acquisition rule, this system, this budget.
Two mechanistic observations point the same direction. The Delta is a sum of radial pair potentials with no angular or many-body terms, while the position and curvature of a cycloaddition saddle depend on angular reorganization of the forming ring. And xTB is never near-stationary at the corrected saddle (0.43–2.81 eV/Å), so force-matching there asks the correction to reproduce a large reference gradient at a point the corrected model believes is stationary — a directly conflicting demand.

What this does and does not claim The behaviour is consistent with a correction-capacity limitation, which motivates a controlled capacity ablation. That is a supported hypothesis, not a demonstrated result — establishing it requires holding the acquisition rule fixed while varying the correction’s expressiveness. This experiment does not show that active learning fails: no acquisition metric, uncertainty estimate, or autonomous sampling was implemented here.

title: Pillar 4 — Iterative correction and reference handoff
text:
Is there a handoff signal?
The follow-up asked whether any property of the starting geometry predicts success. Replicates were run, 14 descriptors were measured for every start, and near-identical starting points were compared.



Left: xTB residual force at the handoff geometry does not separate successes from failures. Right: two near-twin pairs of starting geometries, indistinguishable across the descriptors, with opposite outcomes.



Key result — negative No tested pre-handoff descriptor reliably predicts success. Two pairs of starting geometries separated by only 0.007 Å and 0.022 Å RMSD produce opposite outcomes, with 6–12× cost differences. The intuitive rule fails: the start with the largest xTB residual force (IDPP, 4.99 eV/Å) succeeds, while starts with small residual forces (0.46, 0.69 eV/Å) fail.


Demonstrated The qualitative outcome reproduces across replicates; successful and stalled cases are deterministic, while one failing case dissociates by different routes in each replicate (a flat, dissociative surface amplifying bit-level SCF differences).
Interpretation At the resolution that separates these candidates, the handoff outcome does not behave as a smooth function of the starting state.

title: Pillar 4 — Iterative correction and reference handoff
text:
Next question
Is correction-model capacity the bottleneck? The discriminating experiment holds the acquisition rule fixed and varies expressiveness — angular or three-body terms, a larger cutoff, more radial channels. If a richer correction converges on the same 42-query budget, the ceiling is architectural and an acquisition metric becomes worth building. If it does not, no acquisition function would rescue the loop.
